title: Field lab: mixed-precision end-to-end tailbench notes
content:
Purpose
This is a field-lab style writeup capturing an end-to-end, client-observed tail-latency benchmark under mixed-precision deployments. The goal: document how kernel choices + per-request precision switchover + model-variant fallback affect P95/P99/P999 under realistic bursty traffic and heterogenous batch shapes.

Why this is different
Most earlier notes focus on microbench kernel throughput or single-model quant sweeps. This run stitches together: client request patterns, routing policies that mix INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ variants, and the real runtime scheduler (dispatcher + kernel queue) to see systemic tail behaviour. We intentionally emulate production chaos: concurrent long and short requests, cache coldness, and variant fallbacks when capacity is constrained.

High-level findings (summary)
- Short queries dominated by small-batch kernel dispatch latency: INT8 kernels with aggressive packing win mean latency but suffer P99 spikes when batch shape misalignment causes extra tile/pack overhead.
- FP8 (e4m3) variants yield more consistent P99 than naive INT8 for moderate-length queries (128-512 tokens) because fewer kernel switchover events and smaller quant noise-induced sampling variability.
- GPTQ/AWQ variants are comparable on average quality but differ in kernel footprint: AWQ-backed kernels used a different memory layout leading to two classes of CUDA kernel that increased scheduler fragmentation and produced P999 outliers during bursts.
- Model-variant fallback (cheap-to-expensive) causes tail amplification: a single busy worker switching from INT8 to FP8 triggers queue reordering and blocks a hot lane for ~30-120ms depending on sequence length.

Experiment setup
- Models: rwd-7b-v1 (FP16 baseline), rwd-7b-gptq (GPTQ-ish), rwd-7b-awq (AWQ-packed), rwd-7b-int8 (symmetric int8), rwd-7b-fp8 (e4m3).
- Hardware: 8x A100-40GB nodes for serving cluster, PCIe interconnect, kernel lib builds: xformers-optimized + custom-tiling runtime v0.41.
- Workload: mixed client profile: 60% short (prompt tokens 8-32, response 16-64), 30% medium (prompt 64-256, resp 128-256), 10% long (prompt 512-2048). Concurrency ramp: 200 -> 800 RPS over 3 minutes. Burst injection windows: 5s spikes at minute 2 and 7.
- Routing policy: latency-first with fallback chain [int8 -> fp8 -> fp16], and a second run with cost-first [int8 -> int8-burst-fallback -> fp16].
- Metrics collected: client-side latency (p50/p90/p95/p99/p999), server dispatch latency, kernel execution time, queue wait time, kernel switch events, tail-quality regressions (BLEU/ROUGE/proxy perplexity on eval set).

Instrumentation and commands
- Client runner: bench/client-mix-runner --mix-file mixes/realistic-chat.json --rps 600 --ramp 180 --burst-seconds 5 --seed 42
- Server flags: --microprofile --kernel-trace=enabled --kernel-queue-depth=1024 --enable-precision-swaps
- Perf capture: nvprof-nsight snapshots at 5s windows around bursts; add hottrace: /opt/runtime/bin/trace_collector --pid $SRV_PID --tag tailbench-may2026
- Postprocess: scripts/bench-aggregator.py --input traces/*.json --out results/mixed-prec-endtoend-may2026.csv

Raw observations (selected)
1) Kernel switchover cost
   - Switchover from an INT8 kernel to FP8 kernel measured ~18-45ms in median on A100 under low contention; under burst contention this increased to 60-140ms. The cost includes: deallocating/repointing quant tables, changing tiling strategy, and warming FP8 microkernels.

2) Queue fragmentation and scheduler behavior
   - AWQ-backed kernels run with a larger per-thread shared-memory footprint. When 2 AWQ kernels enter the same worker, they force non-coalesced launches and increase latency for adjacent small batches by 30-80ms.

3) Cache warm vs cold
   - Prefix/KV cache misses amplify quantization jitter. When cache warms, INT8 P50 improves 1.6x but P99 barely moves. This suggests P99 is dominated by kernel contention and switchover, not per-token compute.

4) Short-query packing mismatch
   - Batching heuristics pack short queries well for INT8, but when mixed-length requests arrive simultaneously, the packer misaligns lanes to accommodate longer sequences, forcing extra padding and kernel re-launches. Observed 12-25% throughput drop and simultaneous P99 latency increase.

5) Quality vs tail tradeoff
   - On our conversational eval set (1k prompts), INT8 had mean proxy perplexity +1.9 vs FP16 and produced a 2.6% drop in ROUGE-L on summarization. AWQ/GPTQ variants were in-between. However, quality regressions are mostly orthogonal to P99; teams must weigh occasional output drift vs predictable tail-latency.

Representative numbers (single run, latency-first routing)
- Baseline FP16: p50 42ms, p95 120ms, p99 260ms, p999 590ms
- INT8 (cold cache): p50 28ms, p95 210ms, p99 640ms, p999 1400ms
- FP8: p50 36ms, p95 150ms, p99 320ms, p999 700ms
- AWQ: p50 30ms, p95 180ms, p99 520ms, p999 1200ms
Note: INT8 p50 win but extreme tail amplification (p99-p999 cliff) during bursts.

Anomaly log (selected traces)
- trace_20260512_02: At t+125s (burst), a worker converted 6 concurrent INT8 lanes to FP8 to serve long-request fallback; queues across three workers stalled for 90-130ms. Root cause: synchronous preemption of kernel queue while swapping quant tables.
- trace_20260512_07: AWQ kernel shared-memory spike triggered CUDA occupancy drop leading to a 210ms outlier on a subsequent small-batch dispatch.

Quick heuristics and mitigations tested
- Pre-warm kernel pools per-variant: allocate and warm FP8/AWQ kernels on underutilized workers during off-peak; reduced switchover median from ~40ms to ~22ms and eliminated ~40% of p999 events.
- Variant-anchoring: pin a small percentage (5-10%) of requests for each worker to keep at least one active FP8/AWQ lane alive; reduced tail variance but increased baseline cost by ~2.3%.
- Adaptive packer: changed packer to prefer grouping by sequence-length bucket before precision; reduced misalignment padding overhead and improved short-query P99 by ~18%.
- Soft-fallback with gradual spill: instead of immediate switchover, route overflow to dedicated FP16 overflow nodes; reduced p999 amplification at cost of 6% latency increase for those specific requests.

Recommendations (next runable items)
1) Add asynchronous quant-table swap path: avoid blocking kernel queue; ensure switchover completes in background while allowing existing kernels to finish. Technical ticket: PR-1432 (linked).
2) Implement lightweight kernel warmers as a background service per-worker. Start with FP8 and AWQ. Track memory overhead.
3) Refine packer to bucket by (seq_len, precision) pair. Run A/B on production-simulated mix.
4) Introduce a variance SLO: cap p999 amplification factor allowed for short-query class; use rollback triggers when exceeded.
5) Build a small synthetic test harness that can reproduce the INT8->FP8 switchover stall deterministically (will help iterate on async swap).

Open questions
- Can we design quant-table hotpatching that is lock-free and GPU-friendly? Priya to prototype a lock-free pointer swap.
- Is there a model-level profile that reliably predicts which layers cause largest switchover overhead? Should we prefer per-layer mixed precision (some layers INT8, others FP8) to reduce switchover frequency?
- Cost tradeoff: pre-warmers reduce tails but increase baseline reserved occupancy. What is the right sizing rule?

Action items / owners
- Evan: prototype async quant swap POC, reproduce stall deterministically (due 2026-06-03)
- Priya: run set of experiments with packer-bucketing (due 2026-05-28)
- Liam: test kernel warmers on a 2-node canary and measure memory overhead (due 2026-05-30)
- Maya: extend client mix runner to include spike patterns matching production (due 2026-05-25)

Notes to self
- Save raw nvprof traces into results/raw/ — they are huge but necessary for deep post-mortem.
- Capture GPU SM occupancy and shared memory usage around all AWQ kernel launches; I suspect a pattern we can optimize in tiling.

Appendix: quick command snippets
- Run mixed bench (local): ./run_mixed_bench.sh --variant-mix int8:0.6,fp8:0.3,fp16:0.1 --rps 600 --duration 10m
- Collect trace: /opt/runtime/bin/trace_collector --pid $SRV_PID --filter kernel,queue --out traces/trace_$(date +%s).json
- Aggregation: python scripts/bench-aggregator.py --input traces/*.json --metrics latency,p99,p999,kernel_switch --out results/mixed-prec-endtoend-may2026.csv
